title: The Lion and the Mouse
author: Aesop
body:
Deep in a warm, green forest, a great lion lay sleeping in the shade of a tall tree. His golden mane rose and fell with each slow breath.

A tiny mouse came scurrying through the grass, looking for seeds. She was in such a hurry that she ran right over the lion's big paw. The lion woke with a rumble and caught her gently beneath it.

"Please, Mr. Lion, let me go!" squeaked the mouse. "If you set me free, one day I'll help you."

The lion chuckled. "You? Help me? You're so small!" But he was kind, so he lifted his paw, and the little mouse dashed away.

A few days later, the lion was walking through the forest when he stepped into a hunter's net. The ropes wrapped all around him. He pulled and pushed, but the net only grew tighter. He gave a great, sad roar.

Far away, the little mouse heard him. "That's my friend!" she said, and she ran as fast as her tiny legs could go.

When she found the lion, she began to nibble the ropes. Nibble, nibble, snip. One rope broke, then another, and another, until the lion was free.

The lion looked down at her in surprise. "You did help me," he said softly. "Thank you, little friend."

From that day on, the great lion and the tiny mouse were the best of friends.
moral: No act of kindness is ever wasted, and even the smallest friend can be a great help.

title: The Ugly Duckling
author: Hans Christian Andersen
body:
One summer, beside a quiet pond, a mother duck sat on her nest of eggs. One by one, the eggs cracked open, and out came fluffy yellow ducklings. But the last egg was the biggest, and when it finally hatched, out tumbled a large grey duckling with long legs and a long neck.

"He doesn't look like the others," the farmyard animals whispered. The hens pecked at him, the ducks laughed, and even his brothers and sisters said, "You're so ugly!"

The little grey duckling felt so sad that he ran away. All autumn he wandered through the marshes alone. When winter came, the pond froze, and he huddled in the reeds, cold and lonely.

One day, high in the sky, he saw a flock of beautiful white birds with long, graceful necks. "How lovely they are," he sighed. "I wish I could be like them."

At last, spring arrived. The sun warmed the water, and the duckling stretched his wings. They were strong now! He flew to a sparkling lake, where the white birds were swimming. He bowed his head, sure they would chase him away.

But in the clear water he saw his reflection. He was no longer a grey, clumsy duckling. He was a swan, white and beautiful, just like them.

The other swans swam over and welcomed him. "You're one of us," they said gently. And the young swan felt happier than he had ever dreamed.
moral: Everyone grows in their own way and time, so be kind to those who are different.

title: The Tortoise and the Hare
author: Aesop
body:
Once upon a time, a speedy hare lived at the edge of a big green meadow. He loved to boast. "I'm the fastest animal in the whole world!" he would say, zipping back and forth. "Nobody can beat me!"

One day, a slow and steady tortoise looked up from munching clover. "Would you like to race me?" he asked quietly.

The hare laughed so hard he rolled in the grass. "You? Race me? You're the slowest creature I know! All right, let's race!"

The animals gathered to watch. The fox drew a starting line and pointed to a tall tree far across the meadow. "The first one to reach that tree wins. Ready, set, go!"

Whoosh! The hare shot off like the wind, leaving a cloud of dust behind him. The tortoise began to walk, one small step at a time.

Soon the hare was so far ahead that he couldn't even see the tortoise. "This is too easy," he yawned. "I'll take a little nap under this shady bush. I'll still win." And he fell fast asleep.

Meanwhile, the tortoise kept going. Step, step, step. He didn't stop, and he didn't hurry. He just kept going.

When the hare finally woke up, the sun was low in the sky. He raced toward the tree as fast as he could. But the tortoise was already there, and all the animals were cheering.

The tortoise had won the race.
moral: Slow and steady wins the race, so keep going and never give up.

title: The Crow and the Pitcher
author: Aesop
body:
One very hot summer, a thirsty crow flew across the land looking for water. The rivers were dry. The puddles were gone. His throat felt scratchy and his wings felt tired.

At last he spotted a pitcher beside a house. "Maybe there is water inside!" he thought, and he swooped down.

Yes, there was water in the pitcher, but only a little, right at the bottom. The crow stretched his neck and pushed in his beak, but he could not reach it. He tried to tip the pitcher over, but it was too heavy.

The crow sat and thought. Then he spotted some small pebbles on the ground.

He picked up one pebble and dropped it into the pitcher. Plink! Then he fetched another. Plink! And another. Plink! Plink! Little by little, the water crept higher and higher as the pebbles filled the bottom.

The crow kept going, one pebble at a time, until the water rose right up to the top of the pitcher. Now he could reach it! He took a long, cool drink and felt much better.
moral: When we think carefully and keep trying, a little effort at a time can solve a big problem.

title: The Ant and the Grasshopper
author: Aesop
body:
One warm summer day, a little grasshopper sat in the sunshine, singing and hopping through the green grass. Nearby, an ant marched past, carrying a heavy grain of corn.

"Come and play with me!" called the grasshopper. "Why work so hard on such a lovely day?"

"I am gathering food for the winter," said the ant. "You should do the same."

"Winter is far away," laughed the grasshopper, and he went on singing.

All summer long, the ant worked. Day after day, she carried grains to her snug home underground, until her storeroom was full.

Then the cold winter came. The grass turned brown, and snow covered the ground. The grasshopper was cold and very hungry. He could not find a single seed to eat.

At last he knocked on the ant's door. "Please, could you share some food with me?" he asked softly.

The ant looked at him. "What were you doing all summer?" she asked.

"I was singing," said the grasshopper, hanging his head.

The ant sighed. "Then perhaps now you can learn from this." And in some tellings, she kindly lets him in, so he never forgets to prepare again.
moral: It is wise to work and prepare today for the days that are coming.

title: The Boy Who Cried Wolf
author: Aesop
body:
Once there was a young shepherd boy who looked after his sheep on a green hillside, near a little village. All day he sat watching the sheep, and he grew very bored.

"I know a fun trick," he thought. He jumped up and shouted, "Wolf! Wolf! A wolf is after the sheep!"

The villagers dropped everything and hurried up the hill to help. But there was no wolf. The boy laughed and laughed. The villagers were not happy at all, and they walked back down.

The next day, the boy did it again. "Wolf! Wolf!" he cried. Again the villagers came running, and again there was no wolf. They felt cross and tired.

Then one evening, a real wolf came creeping toward the sheep. The boy was frightened. "Wolf! Wolf! Please help me, a wolf is really here!" he shouted as loudly as he could.

But the villagers shook their heads. "He is playing his trick again," they said, and nobody came.

The wolf frightened the sheep, and they scattered across the hills. At last the boy found them, one by one, and he led them home in the dark, sad and sorry. He had learned that when you tell lies, people stop believing you, even when you finally tell the truth. From then on, he always told the truth.
moral: If you tell lies, people will not believe you, even when you are telling the truth.

title: The Fox and the Grapes
author: Aesop
body:
One warm, sunny afternoon, a hungry fox went walking through the countryside. His tummy rumbled. Grumble, grumble!

Soon he came to a garden wall, and high above his head hung a bunch of plump, purple grapes. They looked juicy and sweet, shining in the sun.

"Oh, what a lovely snack!" said the fox, licking his lips.

He jumped up, but the grapes were too high. He jumped again, higher this time, but he still could not reach them. He took a big run-up and leaped with all his might. Nothing! He tried again and again, until he was puffing and panting.

At last the fox sat down. The grapes still hung far above him.

He looked up and sniffed. "Oh, never mind," he said. "Those grapes are probably sour anyway. I don't want them."

Then he lifted his nose, turned around, and trotted away.
moral: It is easy to pretend we did not want something just because we could not get it, but it is better to be honest about it.

title: The Princess and the Pea
author: Hans Christian Andersen
body:
Once upon a time there was a prince who wanted to marry a princess, but she had to be a real princess. He travelled all over the world to find one. He met many princesses, but each time something didn't seem quite right. So he came home feeling sad, because he wanted a real princess so very much.

One evening there was a terrible storm. Thunder rumbled, lightning flashed, and the rain poured down. Then someone knocked at the city gate, and the old king went to open it.

A princess was standing outside. But oh, what a sight she was! Water ran from her hair and her clothes, into her shoes and out at the heels. Still, she said she was a real princess.

"Well, we'll soon find out," thought the old queen. She didn't say a word. She went into the guest bedroom, took off all the bedding, and put one tiny pea on the bottom of the bed. Then she piled twenty mattresses on top of the pea, and twenty soft feather quilts on top of the mattresses. That was where the princess slept that night.

In the morning they asked her how she had slept.

"Oh, terribly!" said the princess. "I hardly closed my eyes all night. There was something hard in my bed, and now I'm black and blue all over!"

Then everyone knew she was a real princess, because only a real princess could feel one little pea through twenty mattresses and twenty feather quilts.

So the prince married her, and the pea was put in a museum, where you can still see it, unless someone has taken it!
moral: What makes a person special isn't always what you can see on the outside.

title: The North Wind and the Sun
author: Aesop
body:
One day, the North Wind and the Sun began to argue about which of them was stronger.

"I am much stronger than you," puffed the North Wind.

"Let's find out," said the Sun kindly. Just then, a traveller came walking down the road, wrapped in a warm cloak.

"Whoever can make that traveller take off his cloak is the stronger one," said the Sun. "You may go first."

So the North Wind took a deep breath and blew. Whoosh! He blew harder and harder. The trees bent and the leaves flew everywhere. But the colder the wind blew, the tighter the traveller pulled his cloak around himself. At last the North Wind grew tired and gave up.

Then it was the Sun's turn. The Sun came out from behind a cloud and shone gently down on the traveller. Slowly the air grew warm. The traveller loosened his cloak. The Sun shone a little warmer, and soon the traveller felt so hot that he took his cloak off and sat down in the shade of a tree to rest.

The North Wind had to agree that the Sun had won, not by being rough, but by being gentle and warm.
moral: Kindness and gentleness can do what force and anger cannot.
